# Perdition Gulch

## I.

The council met, as it always met, in the back room of Drury's dry-goods store, at a table Drury had built from railroad ties he'd scavenged before the railroad decided it wanted to come through after all. Five chairs. Five cups. A plate of biscuits the healer had made that morning because he'd read in a pamphlet from St. Louis that sodium powder was eroding the constitution of the American settlement, and he had taken it upon himself to bake without it. The biscuits were flat and gray and no one touched them.

"It's the Gunderson boy," said the memory-keeper. Her name was Pauline Bray, and she sat at the head of the table because no one had ever sat there before her, and because the records—all of them, every survey, every birth, every water claim—were in her journals, and the journals were in her house, and her house was at the center of town. "His mother has come to me about the fever. He's had it nine days."

"I'll go this afternoon," said the healer. His name was Otis Fleet. He'd been a farrier in another life, before Perdition Gulch, and his hands were still enormous, scarred across the palms in the shape of old horseshoes. He turned them over on the table now, absently, as though checking that the scars were still there. They were.

"Nine days is long," said one of the twins.

"Nine days is nothing," said the other.

The twins were Marah and Lesta Coe. They sat beside each other, always, close enough that their elbows touched, and they spoke in a way that had long ceased to unsettle the council but that never failed to unsettle anyone else: one beginning a sentence, the other finishing it, or both saying the same word at the same instant, or one falling silent at the precise moment the other needed silence. They were forty-seven years old. They had never spent a night in separate rooms.

"And the water," said Pauline. She opened a journal—this year's, with its green leather cover—and ran her finger down a column of figures. "The Alderton well is drawing six inches lower than this time last year. I've noted the rate of decline and the aquifer line from the territorial survey of—" She paused. Her finger stopped. "The survey of sixty-eight," she said, but the pause had lasted one beat longer than a pause should last in the mouth of a woman who had never, in the memory of anyone at the table, paused.

"Sixty-eight?" said Otis.

"The August survey. Cavanaugh and—" Another pause. Pauline looked at the journal. The name was not in the journal. The name was in her, or had been, the way every name was in her: the surveyor's assistant who had come through with a theodolite and a cough and had stayed three days and measured the depth of every water source within four miles of the town marker. She could see the theodolite. She could see the cough—the way the man had pressed a handkerchief to his mouth and the handkerchief had come away spotted. She could see his boots, which were eastern boots, cracked at the toe. She could not see his face.

"Cavanaugh and Whiting," said the child.

The child was not a child. She was thirty-one years old. Her name was Dessa Rae Calloway, and she had been nine when the council formed, and she had been called the child then, and the name had never corrected itself. She sat at the foot of the table, the farthest chair, the one backed against the wall, and she spoke less than anyone because she heard more. What she heard was not sound. What she heard was the interiors of other people, the unspoken, the raw thought before it became language, the want before it became request. She had heard Pauline's mind go looking for the name and come back empty, and she had supplied it the way one hands a dropped tool back to its owner: without comment, without emphasis.

"Whiting," said Pauline. "Yes. Of course. Cavanaugh and Whiting."

The council looked at her. The council did not look at each other.

"The biscuits," said Otis, "are also a matter I'd like to raise. Sodium powder. I have the pamphlet."

"You've brought the pamphlet before," said Marah.

"Three times," said Lesta.

"The pamphlet is not new information," they said, not together but in a braid, Marah's words filling the spaces between Lesta's, so that the sentence assembled itself across two mouths like a rope across two hands.

Pauline closed the journal. "Sodium powder can wait," she said. She did not say: *I couldn't see his face.* She did not think it loudly enough for Dessa to hear, or she thought she didn't, but Dessa heard it anyway—not as words but as the particular color of fear that belongs to a person who has built a life on the certainty that she will never lose a single thing and has just felt the first thing go.

The biscuits sat on the plate. The light through the window was the light of late October in the high desert, which is to say it was the color of bone.

"The Gunderson boy," said Pauline. "Otis, go this afternoon. And the Alderton well. I'll draft the rationing tiers tonight."

The council rose. Five chairs pushed back. Five cups, barely touched. The door opened onto the single street that was Perdition Gulch—forty buildings, a hundred and twelve souls, one road in, the same road out, the canyon to the south where the road bent and the walls rose high enough to hold an echo.

---

The ridge had no name. It was a spine of sandstone running east to west above the canyon's northern rim, and on the morning of September 14, 1857, five people stood on it and looked down.

The wagon train was visible from two miles out: nine wagons, standard Conestoga configuration, ox-drawn, moving at the pace of beasts that had been moving for months and saw no reason this month should differ from the last. Pauline had counted the wagons three days ago, when the train had passed through the flats to the east, and she had counted the people—forty-one adults, nineteen children, four infants she could identify by the particular way the women held their left arms—and she had estimated their route based on the creekbed they were following, which would bring them, inevitably, to the canyon's southern mouth.

The outlaws had been in the canyon for two days. Seven men. Pauline could tell the council their names, the provenance of their horses, the makes of their rifles. Dessa, who was nine, who stood between Marah and Lesta with her hands pressed over her ears in a gesture that accomplished nothing because what she heard did not enter through her ears, could tell the council what the men intended. She had been hearing them since they arrived—their plans, their appetites, the specific arithmetic of what nine wagons might yield in goods and what forty-one adults minus the men might yield in other currencies. She had told Pauline. Pauline had written it down.

"Seven," said Marah.

"Seven is manageable," said Lesta.

"The south mouth is thirty yards wide," said Pauline. She did not open a journal. She did not need to. "Rock cover on both sides to a height of nine feet, adequate for two positions. The bend at forty yards creates a blind approach from the north. If two people entered from the north rim and two from the south, the seven would be exposed on three sides with retreat only to the east, where the wash narrows to twelve feet and a single person could hold it."

"I could hold it," said Otis. He said this simply. He had been shot twice in the years before Perdition Gulch—once in Virginia, once on the trail—and both times his body had done what his body did: closed around the bullet like water around a stone, pushed the lead out through the entry wound, sealed the skin in the time it took to draw a breath. He did not know why. He had never known why. He knew only that he could stand in a twelve-foot wash and be shot and continue standing, and that this fact, which had once terrified him, had become a kind of tool, the way Pauline's memory was a tool, the way the child's hearing was a tool.

"The angle from the north rim is seventeen degrees," Pauline continued. "At that angle, rifle fire into the canyon floor would require—"

"They're going to kill everyone," said the child.

She said it flatly, without the drama that a nine-year-old's voice should carry when reporting the intentions of seven armed men toward sixty people. She said it the way she said everything she heard: as fact, as data, as something that existed in the world independent of her and passed through her the way light passes through glass.

"We know," said Pauline.

"The children too," said Dessa. "They've decided about the children."

The wind moved across the ridge. Below, in the canyon, seven men waited in positions that Pauline could have mapped from memory, at distances she could have stated to the foot. Two miles south, the wagon train moved north.

"The question," said Pauline, and she said it in the same register she would use, decades later, to discuss sodium powder and well levels and rationing tiers, "is exposure. If we intervene, we are seen. Forty-one adults survive, and forty-one adults know what we can do. The child hears thoughts. The twins share a mind. I forget nothing. Otis cannot be killed. We've discussed what that knowledge does when it reaches a settlement. When it reaches a territory. When it reaches anyone with the authority to study or contain or use."

"We've discussed it," said Otis.

"The probability of containment is low," said Pauline. "Even if the survivors are disposed to gratitude—and gratitude is not the typical response to the uncanny—word travels. It has always traveled."

"We could ask them not to tell," said the child.

No one answered this. Not because it was foolish but because it was nine years old, and because the five of them had not yet learned how to explain to a nine-year-old that the world does not keep promises, that the five of them had come to this territory specifically because the world had failed to keep promises about what would be done to people like them, and that the canyon below was not the first canyon, and the seven men were not the first men, and the question was never whether to do good but whether the doing of good would end in a room with a lock and a doctor who wanted to see what was inside them.

"If we go down there," said Marah.

"We lose this," said Lesta.

"The town. The distance. The ordinary life," they said together, and the ordinary life meant the life they had built in nine months—the forty buildings, the wells, the school where Dessa pretended to learn things she already knew from hearing the teacher's mind—and it meant the distance between themselves and every other place, which was the distance between being people and being specimens.

Pauline looked at the canyon. She looked at the wagon train. She looked at the ridge where five people stood whose combined capabilities could have cleared the canyon in four minutes—she had calculated it, because she calculated everything, because the calculation was the only way she knew to hold a thing at arm's length and keep it from becoming a feeling.

"The approach time for the train to the canyon mouth is approximately ninety minutes," she said. "At current pace. Accounting for a rest stop at the creek, which the lead driver will likely take, two hours."

"Two hours," said Otis.

"Yes."

"And the exposure radius, if we're seen—"

"Uncontainable. As I've said."

Otis looked at his hands. The scars from the horseshoes. He pressed one thumb into the opposite palm, testing—though not testing, really, because there was nothing to test; the ability was constant, had always been constant—and the flesh yielded and did not break, as it always yielded and did not break. He was invulnerable. He could walk into a canyon and receive seven rifles' worth of fire and absorb it the way the desert absorbed rain, and the cost would be nothing to his body and everything to the life he'd built, and the people in the wagons would live, and the life would be over.

"We should vote," said Pauline.

They voted. Pauline recorded the vote, as she recorded everything, and the vote was unanimous, and the specific words each person used when casting it—the euphemisms, the indirections, the careful language of *strategic withdrawal* and *long-term preservation* and *the greater protection of what we've built*—these were words that Dessa heard under and around and through, and what she heard beneath them was not anguish and not conflict and not even the particular tortured calculus of people doing wrong in full knowledge of its wrongness.

What she heard was relief.

A settling. A permission. The sound the mind makes when it has been given a reason not to do the hard thing and has accepted the reason and now, having accepted it, feels the muscles of obligation relax one by one, the way a fist opens and becomes a hand and the hand does not shake because the fist had already decided.

Five people stood on the ridge. Below them, in the canyon, seven men checked their rifles. Two miles south, the wagon train moved north. The light was the light of September in the high desert, which is indistinguishable from the light of October, which is indistinguishable from the light of any other month in a place where the sky does not soften.

They walked back to town. They walked single file, the way they'd come, Pauline leading, the child at the rear. The trail descended the north face of the ridge and joined the main road half a mile from the first building, and by the time they reached the road they could no longer see the canyon, and by the time they reached the first building they could no longer see the ridge.

The sounds carried anyway. They carried for what Pauline estimated to be eleven minutes, though she did not estimate this at the time—she held the number without choosing to, the way she held every number, every face, every angle of approach—and the sounds were of the kind that did not require supernatural hearing to interpret, so that Dessa, walking at the rear with her hands at her sides because the gesture of covering her ears had never accomplished anything, heard them twice: once through the air, the way anyone hears, and once through the minds of the forty-one adults and nineteen children for whom the sounds were not distant but immediate, not acoustic but physical, and then through fewer minds, and then fewer, and then through minds that were not thinking in words anymore but in colors she did not have names for, and then through very few, and then she heard the seven men again, only the seven, their thoughts collapsing back to the ordinary—to hunger, to logistics, to the arithmetic of what the wagons held—in a way that was worse than what had come before because it was quieter.

The council convened that evening. Five chairs. Five cups. The same table. Pauline read the minutes of the vote. Otis reported on the Gunderson well, which was producing adequately. Marah and Lesta proposed a schedule for the autumn harvest. The child sat at the foot of the table and said nothing, because she had never said much, because when you can hear everything there is very little reason to speak, and because the sounds from the canyon were still in her—not as echoes but as residents, as tenants who had moved into a room in her mind and would not leave, and she was nine, and she did not yet understand that they would never leave, that she would carry them for twenty-two years in silence, that the silence would become the thing people knew about her and mistook for disposition.

The minutes were approved. The meeting adjourned. Five chairs pushed back. The door opened onto the single street, and the street was dark, and the dark was the same dark that covered the canyon two miles south, where nine wagons stood in a configuration that Pauline could have diagrammed from memory but did not, and would not, and filed instead in the place where she filed things that were not to be retrieved but could not be discarded, a place she thought of as the back shelf, the high shelf, the shelf she did not need a ladder to reach because she could reach anything, because that was what she was, that was the justification, that was the reason five people with extraordinary capabilities could stand on a ridge and calculate angles and vote and walk home: because they were extraordinary, and extraordinary people make extraordinary calculations, and the calculation had been sound, and the town was intact, and the secret was the mortar, and the mortar would hold.
